scenes.heading: BigQuery Architecture (Dremel & Slots)
scenes.narration: BigQuery is serverless, running queries on Google's Dremel engine with compute measured in units called slots.

scenes.heading: The building blocks
bullets: Dremel: the distributed engine that executes queries as an execution tree.
Colossus: Google's storage layer holding columnar data in Capacitor format.
Jupiter: the petabit network that shuffles data between compute and storage.
Slots: virtual CPUs that represent your unit of query compute.
scenes.narration: Dremel breaks each query into a tree of parallel stages that fan work out and aggregate results back. Data lives separately in Colossus using the columnar Capacitor format, connected by the ultra-fast Jupiter network. Slots are the abstract compute units BigQuery allocates to run your query stages.

scenes.heading: How Dremel executes a query
scenes.narration: A query enters at the root, which divides it among mixer nodes. Those mixers push shards down to leaf nodes that read the columnar data straight from Colossus. Partial results then bubble back up the tree, aggregating at each level into the final answer.

scenes.heading: On-demand vs capacity pricing

right.title: Capacity (reservations)
points: Buy slots for a fixed price

scenes.narration: On-demand pricing charges by the bytes each query scans, which is simple and ideal for unpredictable workloads. Capacity pricing buys a reserved pool of slots at a flat rate for cost predictability. Choose on-demand for bursty analytics and reservations once usage is large and steady.

scenes.text: BigQuery is serverless: Dremel executes as a tree, Colossus stores columnar data, and slots meter your compute.
scenes.narration: With no clusters to manage, you just think about slots and bytes scanned while Dremel and Colossus do the heavy lifting.
